content: An oral ulcer, also known as an ulceration of the oral mucosa, is an open sore that develops inside the mouth due to a disruption in the mucous membrane or epithelial lining. These lesions can occur on the lips, inner cheeks, tongue, or other areas within the oral cavity. The causes of oral ulcers are varied and include physical or chemical trauma, infections (bacterial, viral, or fungal), systemic medical conditions, medications, malignancies, and sometimes idiopathic processes. Once an ulcer forms, it may persist due to ongoing inflammation or secondary infection. Two of the most common types of oral ulcers are aphthous ulcers (commonly referred to as canker sores) and cold sores, which are caused by the herpes simplex virus. Causes of Oral Ulcers Common Causes Oral ulcers can arise from numerous factors, including immune system dysregulation, physical trauma, nutritional deficiencies, and certain medications. Stress, fatigue, illness, accidental biting, hormonal fluctuations (e.g., during menstruation), sudden weight loss, food allergies, and deficiencies in vitamin B12, iron, or folic acid are all known triggers. Some medications, such as nicorandil, and recreational drugs have also been implicated in the development of oral ulcers. Additionally, excessive consumption of acidic or sour foods can contribute to ulcer formation. Trauma-Related Causes Minor Physical Injuries: Physical trauma is a frequent cause of oral ulcers. This can result from sharp teeth, accidental biting (especially involving sharp canine teeth), abrasive or sharp foods, poorly fitting dentures, dental braces, or improper use of a toothbrush. These ulcers typically heal once the source of the trauma is removed or corrected. Chemical Injuries: Certain chemicals, such as aspirin or alcohol, when held in contact with the oral mucosa, can cause tissue necrosis, leading to ulceration. Sodium lauryl sulfate (SLS), a common ingredient in many toothpastes, has been associated with an increased incidence of oral ulcers. Infectious Causes Viral Infections: The herpes simplex virus is the most common viral cause of oral ulcers, presenting as painful vesicles that rupture to form ulcers. Other viral causes include herpes zoster (shingles), varicella zoster (chickenpox), and Coxsackie A virus. In individuals with HIV, immunodeficiency can lead to opportunistic infections or neoplasms that manifest as oral ulcers. Bacterial Infections: Bacterial pathogens such as Mycobacterium tuberculosis (tuberculosis) and Treponema pallidum (syphilis) can cause oral ulceration. Additionally, opportunistic overgrowth of normal oral flora, including species like Streptococci, Neisseria, Actinomyces, spirochetes, and Bacteroides, can exacerbate or prolong ulcerative processes. Fungal Infections: Fungal pathogens such as Coccidioides immitis (valley fever), Cryptococcus neoformans (cryptococcosis), and Blastomyces dermatitidis (North American blastomycosis) are less common but can also lead to oral ulceration. Immune System-Related Causes Immune Dysregulation: Aphthous ulcers are thought to result from immune-mediated processes, where the body reacts to unrecognized molecules, triggering lymphocyte activation and subsequent tissue damage. Immunodeficiency: Recurrent oral ulcers may indicate an underlying immunodeficiency, such as low immunoglobulin levels in the oral mucosa. Conditions like HIV and chemotherapy-induced immunosuppression are common causes of such ulcers. Autoimmune Disorders: Autoimmune conditions, such as mucous membrane pemphigoid, involve an immune response against the epithelial basement membrane, leading to desquamation and ulceration of the oral mucosa. Allergic Reactions: Contact with allergens can also result in mucosal ulceration. Dietary and Nutritional Factors Vitamin Deficiencies: Deficiencies in vitamin C (leading to scurvy), vitamin B12, iron, zinc, and folic acid are associated with impaired wound healing and the development of oral ulcers. Celiac Disease: Gluten intolerance, as seen in celiac disease, can cause chronic oral ulcers. Avoiding gluten-containing foods such as wheat, rye, and barley is essential for prevention. Artificial Sweeteners: Certain artificial sweeteners, such as those found in diet sodas and sugar-free gum, have been reported to cause oral ulcers in some individuals. Malignancy Oral cancers, such as squamous cell carcinoma, can present as ulcerative lesions. These ulcers often result from necrosis of the lesion's center due to inadequate blood supply. Symptoms of Oral Ulcers The initial symptoms of an oral ulcer may include a sharp stinging or burning sensation at the site of the future lesion. Within a few days, this area may develop into a red spot or bump, eventually progressing to an open ulcer. The ulcer typically appears as a white or yellow oval lesion with an inflamed red border. A white halo or ring may sometimes surround the lesion. The central area of the ulcer is often covered by fibrin, a protein involved in blood clotting, giving it a grey, white, or yellow appearance. Oral ulcers are frequently painful, particularly when irritated by food, beverages, or mechanical contact. In some cases, painful swelling of the lymph nodes beneath the jaw may occur, which can be mistaken for toothache. Additionally, surrounding areas of the mouth may become inflamed, presenting as rough, red patches. Any oral lesion that persists for more than two weeks should be evaluated by a healthcare professional, as it may indicate a more serious condition, such as oral cancer. Treatment of Oral Ulcers Effective treatment of oral ulcers often requires addressing the underlying cause. For ulcers related to nutritional deficiencies, correcting imbalances in vitamins and minerals can reduce the frequency and severity of ulceration. In cases of trauma-induced ulcers, removing or avoiding the source of injury (e.g., replacing poorly fitting dentures) is essential, though accidental trauma is often unavoidable. For individuals prone to secondary bacterial infections following oral injuries, rinsing the affected area with an antibacterial mouthwash can help prevent infection. This should be done within three hours of the injury and repeated every 12 hours for two days. It is important to use a small amount of mouthwash (approximately 1 mL) to minimize potential side effects, such as altered taste perception or disruption of the normal oral flora. Following the manufacturer's instructions for subsequent rinses is also recommended.
